strengths: The paper addresses a timely and useful problem: combining semantic alignment from VLMs with visually discriminative features from VFMs for transductive zero-shot classification, without gradient-based adaptation.

The proposed framework is simple and practically appealing: extract CLIP probabilities, fit/update GMM-style visual posteriors on VFM features, and fuse them through an iterative assignment procedure. This makes the method potentially easy to deploy compared with prompt tuning or test-time training methods.

The empirical evaluation spans 11 common zero-shot benchmarks and reports large average improvements over vanilla CLIP for both ViT-B/16 and ResNet-50 CLIP backbones, with especially strong gains on EuroSAT, Flowers102, ImageNet, Pets, and UCF101.

The ablations are useful in showing that visual features, especially DINOv2 features, are the dominant source of improvement, and that iterative coupling between the fused assignments and GMM updates improves over a non-joint variant.
weaknesses: The technical formulation of the claimed optimal transport objective appears mathematically inconsistent. The stated constraint Q 1_K = 1_N and Q^T 1_N = 1_K is infeasible unless the number of samples equals the number of classes, since the total row mass and column mass differ. A transductive test set generally has N much larger than K. This is not a presentation nit: it affects the definition of the optimization problem and the meaning of the Sinkhorn updates.

The method is described as minimizing transport cost, but the actual objective is a maximization of linear agreement with probability matrices plus entropy, with no explicit transport cost matrix or distance between distributions. This makes the “optimal transport” interpretation under-specified and somewhat overstated.

Several equations have apparent dimension or notation issues. For example, Q is defined as N x K, but the Sinkhorn scaling in Eq. 8-10 uses u in R^K and v in R^N with diagonal multiplications that do not align as written. The paper also alternates between K and C for class count and between feature variables z, v, and X in ways that make reproduction difficult.

The ablation weakens the central contribution: DINOv2-only already reaches 74.20 average accuracy, while OTFusion reaches 74.95, and simple feature concatenation reaches 75.54, higher than the proposed fusion. The paper argues distribution fusion is more scalable, but does not provide runtime, memory, or scaling experiments to support this advantage.

The experimental comparison omits important simple baselines, such as probability averaging, weighted averaging tuned on no labels, CLIP-seeded GMM without OT terminology, nearest-cluster/class-prior variants, and label propagation on DINOv2 features. Without these, it is hard to isolate whether the gains come from the proposed fusion objective or from using strong DINOv2 transductive clustering initialized by CLIP.

The transductive setup appears to impose global mass conservation or balanced assignments, but the paper does not discuss class imbalance, real test-set priors, or whether benchmark test splits are approximately balanced. If the method assumes uniform class counts, that can be a strong hidden prior and may limit usefulness in realistic open-world or long-tailed settings.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The paper gives some hyperparameters, hardware, and backbone choices, but lacks precise prompts per dataset, GMM initialization details, covariance regularization, iteration/stopping criteria, Sinkhorn normalization details, random seed handling, preprocessing details beyond center crop, and whether reported numbers are averaged across runs. Code is only promised after acceptance.

The claims of model-agnostic multi-VFM/VLM fusion and compatibility with training-based methods are only partially supported. The main experiments appear to use CLIP plus DINOv2, and the claimed hybrid boosts with methods like Lafter/CPL are not reported in the shown results.

Presentation has multiple clarity issues, including “joint-learning” terminology for a training-free iterative inference method, claims that the loss “increases” during convergence while being optimized as a maximization, and several typos or inconsistent dataset/method names. These are secondary to the correctness concerns but add friction.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem: exploiting unlabeled test distributions and complementary CLIP/DINO-style representations for transductive zero-shot classification is potentially useful.

The method is simple and computationally plausible in spirit: fit visual clusters over foundation-model features, combine them with VLM semantic scores, and solve an entropy-regularized assignment problem.

The empirical section covers 11 common image classification datasets and includes comparisons with several recent CLIP adaptation/transductive methods, plus ablations for semantic-only, visual-only, concatenation, and joint optimization variants.

The reported gains over vanilla CLIP are large on several datasets, especially EuroSAT and Flowers102, suggesting that transductive visual clustering can be a strong signal when the class structure is visually separable.
weaknesses: The mathematical formulation appears technically flawed. The stated constraint Q 1_K = 1_N and Q^T 1_N = 1_K is infeasible for rectangular N-by-K assignments unless N=K, because the row and column marginals imply different total mass. This is not a minor notation issue: the Sinkhorn update and the claimed doubly stochastic transport plan are central to the method.

The proposed objective is not convincingly an optimal transport formulation. It maximizes linear agreement with P and Y plus entropy, but no transport cost between distributions is clearly defined, and P/Y are already class-score matrices rather than measures with specified marginals. The paper repeatedly claims minimization of transport cost, but the actual equations are closer to entropy-regularized soft assignment or balanced clustering.

The main empirical claim is weakened by an unfair comparison setup. OTFusion adds DINOv2 ViT-L/14 features, while many baselines are CLIP-only methods; the ResNet50 table still appears to use DINOv2 as the visual prior. Thus the large improvements over CLIP and CLIP-adaptation baselines may mostly reflect adding a stronger visual foundation model rather than the proposed fusion mechanism.

The ablation undercuts the novelty: DINOv2-only already reaches 74.20 average accuracy versus 74.95 for OTFusion, and simple feature concatenation reaches 75.54, higher than the proposed distribution-fusion method. This suggests the core OT fusion contributes little beyond visual clustering, and the paper does not adequately explain why the proposed method is preferable if a simpler baseline is stronger.

The evaluation lacks important controls: no comparison to a straightforward ensemble of CLIP probabilities and DINO/GMM posteriors, no balanced clustering baseline, no k-means/prototype matching alternative, no label-propagation baseline using the same DINOv2 features, and no runtime/memory comparison despite scalability claims.

Reproducibility is limited. The code is promised only after acceptance; exact preprocessing, prompts, class-name choices, hyperparameter selection protocol, Sinkhorn marginal normalization, GMM covariance details, initialization, number of iterations, and dataset splits are not specified enough to reproduce the results confidently.

The transductive setting is not carefully qualified. The method appears to use the full test set, the number of classes, and possibly balanced class-mass constraints; the paper does not discuss sensitivity to class imbalance, missing classes, batch/subset inference, or realistic deployment where the test distribution may not match the benchmark protocol.

Some claims are overstated relative to the evidence. The paper claims flexible integration of arbitrary VLMs/VFMs and compatibility with training-based methods, but experiments only demonstrate a narrow CLIP plus DINOv2 setup and do not evaluate hybrid training-based use.

Presentation issues further reduce confidence: there are notation inconsistencies between C and K, z/v feature variables, maximization versus minimization language, dimension errors in Sinkhorn scaling vectors, awkward phrasing, and several table/text inconsistencies. These are not merely cosmetic because they obscure what was actually implemented.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and timely problem: improving transductive zero-shot classification by combining the semantic alignment of VLMs with the stronger visual clustering behavior of VFMs. The training-free framing is practically attractive.

The empirical evaluation is broad, covering 11 standard datasets and two CLIP backbones. The reported gains over vanilla CLIP are large on average, especially on datasets such as EuroSAT, Flowers102, ImageNet, and UCF101.

The ablation study is useful and unusually revealing: it separates semantic-only, CLIP-visual-only, DINOv2-only, concatenation, no joint learning, and the proposed fusion, which helps identify where the improvements come from.
The method is conceptually simple and modular. Operating in probability space could make it easy to plug in different foundation models without retraining large networks.
The paper includes parameter sensitivity and convergence analyses, which support the claim that the method is relatively stable for the tested hyperparameter ranges.
weaknesses: The technical formulation has a serious issue: the stated transport polytope uses Q 1_K = 1_N and Q^T 1_N = 1_K for Q in R^{N x K}. These constraints imply total mass N from rows and K from columns, which is infeasible unless N = K. The Sinkhorn update dimensions also appear inconsistent. This may be a notation error, but as written the core optimization is not technically correct.

The evidence for the specific OT fusion contribution is weaker than the headline results suggest. In Table 2, DINOv2-only already reaches 74.20 average versus 74.95 for OTFusion, and simple feature concatenation reaches 75.54, exceeding OTFusion. Thus much of the gain appears to come from using DINOv2/GMM transductive clustering rather than the proposed OT fusion mechanism.

The comparison to prior methods may not be fully fair because OTFusion uses an additional strong DINOv2 ViT-L/14 visual foundation model, while many baselines are CLIP-only adaptation methods. The paper should more clearly distinguish gains from adding a stronger auxiliary model from gains due to the proposed fusion algorithm.

The method relies on the full unlabeled test distribution and on class-count style mass constraints, but the paper does not sufficiently discuss behavior under class imbalance, partial class presence, streaming inference, or distribution shift within the test set. These are important for transductive methods.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The code is only promised after acceptance, and details such as exact dataset splits, preprocessing for all datasets, prompt templates, GMM initialization/regularization, convergence criteria, and hyperparameter selection protocol are not fully specified.

Some claims are overstated relative to the evidence. The paper claims compatibility with training-based pseudo-label methods and performance boosts in hybrid scenarios, but the presented experiments do not appear to substantiate this claim.

Presentation quality is generally understandable but has several issues: notation alternates between C and K for classes, some equations and variables are underspecified, and there are typographical/formatting problems that make the method harder to verify. These are secondary to the technical and empirical concerns above.

strengths: The paper tackles a timely and useful problem: improving zero-shot classification by combining complementary foundation models rather than adapting a single VLM. The idea of using VFM visual structure to correct VLM semantic predictions is well motivated by the observed clustering behavior.

The empirical coverage is broad, spanning 11 natural image datasets, 10 remote sensing datasets, and 5 medical pathology datasets, with both transductive and inductive settings. Reported gains are often large, especially when CLIP is combined with DINOv2/DINOv3 or domain-specific VLMs.

The method is appealingly simple at a high level: convert model outputs to probability/cost matrices, fuse them through entropic OT, and use the resulting transport plan directly or as supervision for GMM-based inductive inference.

The paper includes useful ablations for VFM introduction, adaptive weighting, and joint learning, plus convergence and efficiency analyses. These support the claim that visual foundation features are a major source of improvement.
The proposed approach is potentially useful in practice because it does not require gradient updates to the foundation models and can in principle work with black-box model outputs.
weaknesses: The technical formulation has several important ambiguities and inconsistencies. The OT problem requires target marginals/class priors, yet the paper claims to be prior-free and does not clearly specify how class marginals are set or how robustness to class imbalance is handled. Uniform marginals would be a strong hidden assumption for many real datasets.

The VFM-to-class alignment mechanism is under-specified. A GMM over visual features gives clusters, not semantic class assignments; the paper relies on coupling with VLM outputs but does not clearly explain initialization, cluster-class identifiability, or failure modes when VLM predictions are weak.

There are mathematical and notation errors that affect confidence in the method description: the Sinkhorn update dimensions in the appendix appear swapped, Eq. 19 uses an undefined denominator Q(t), the covariance update is inconsistent with the class-specific covariance notation, and Algorithm 1 conflates VFM and VLM feature/posterior updates.

The core novelty of the self-adaptive weighting is somewhat modest. The squared inner-product objective effectively induces weights proportional to agreement with the current transport plan, but the reported gain from adaptivity itself is small in the main ablation compared with the gain from adding stronger visual encoders.

Some comparisons are not fully balanced. Several SOTA rows use additional models such as DINOv3 or multiple foundation models, while many baselines adapt a single CLIP model. Thus part of the improvement may come from extra model capacity or stronger pretrained features rather than the proposed OT fusion alone.

Remote sensing and medical main comparisons are relatively narrow, mostly emphasizing TransCLIP, while newer or stronger adaptation/ensemble baselines are not consistently reported at the per-dataset level. Table 6 is helpful but insufficient to fully establish superiority across those domains.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The abstract says code is available but the link is blank; key implementation details such as GMM initialization, covariance type/regularization, Sinkhorn iterations, temperature tau, exact marginals, dataset splits, and prompt templates are either missing or deferred to unavailable code.

The inductive setting is potentially confusing: the method uses unlabeled training data to learn GMM parameters and adaptive coefficients, but the paper does not clearly separate this from test-time/transductive adaptation or discuss how sensitive performance is to train-test distribution shift.

Presentation is generally readable, but several claims are overstated, especially “prior-free,” “without hyperparameter adjustment,” and “first work to systematically investigate” multi-foundation-model complementarity, given related ensemble, transductive, and OT-based adaptation literature.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem: improving zero-shot classification by combining multiple foundation models rather than relying on a single VLM. This is a useful direction, especially across natural, remote sensing, and pathology domains where model strengths differ.

The framework is conceptually simple and modular: convert model outputs into probability/cost matrices, fuse them with entropic optimal transport, and optionally use the resulting soft assignments to guide GMM-based visual classifiers.

The experimental scope is broad in number of datasets: 11 natural image datasets, 10 remote sensing datasets, and 5 medical/pathology datasets. The reported gains over individual models are often large.
The paper includes ablations for VFM use, adaptive weighting, joint learning, convergence, and model subsets, which helps identify where some of the gains may come from.
weaknesses: The main technical formulation has serious ambiguities and likely correctness issues. The OT target marginal q is essential but not specified in a way consistent with the paper's claim of being prior-free. If q is uniform, the method imposes a class-balance prior, which can strongly affect accuracy and may explain large gains on balanced benchmarks while failing on imbalanced distributions.

The optimization derivation is not convincing. The MM minorization is applied to squared inner products, but the subsequent GMM update is described as an EM-style M-step for mixture likelihood, not as an update that necessarily maximizes the stated surrogate involving <T, Pv(Theta)>. Therefore the claimed monotonic improvement and convergence to a stationary point are not adequately supported.

There are notation and dimensional inconsistencies in the optimization section, including swapped p/q dimensions in the Sinkhorn update, an undefined Q in the GMM mean denominator, and Algorithm 1 treating VLMs and VFMs similarly despite only VFMs having GMM posteriors. These are not just presentation issues because they obscure the actual algorithm needed to reproduce the method.

The comparison is not clean enough to support the claimed contribution. On natural images, the strongest variants use DINOv2/DINOv3 visual features while many baselines are CLIP adaptation methods, so the gains conflate the proposed OT fusion with access to stronger visual encoders. For remote sensing and medical datasets, the paper compares mainly to TransCLIP rather than a broader set of recent adaptation/ensemble baselines.

The core novelty is limited. Squared-score adaptive weighting, entropic OT, transductive label correction, GMM clustering, and ensemble fusion are all established ingredients. The paper does not sufficiently distinguish its method from simpler alternatives such as averaging calibrated probabilities, clustering-plus-Hungarian alignment, per-model TransCLIP followed by ensembling, or learned/validation-free confidence weighting.

The ablations do not fully isolate the important factors. The largest gains appear to come from introducing strong VFM features, while the self-adaptive component gives small improvements in Figure 4 and Table 5. There is no sensitivity analysis for entropy epsilon, class marginal q, initialization, number of Sinkhorn iterations, GMM covariance structure, feature normalization, or prompt template.

The transductive setting uses the entire test set during inference, but the practical implications and fairness of this assumption are under-discussed. The inductive setting is also unclear: it appears to learn from unlabeled training data drawn from the same label set/distribution, which is a stronger assumption than standard zero-shot classification and should be separated more carefully from test-time adaptation.

Reproducibility is weak. The abstract contains an empty code link, dataset templates are said to be in the code, and important implementation choices are underspecified, including class marginals, initialization, GMM covariance details, Sinkhorn iterations, stopping criteria, random seeds, exact splits, prompt strings, and how reported averages are computed.

The empirical evidence lacks uncertainty estimates and failure analysis. No standard deviations, multiple runs, significance tests, or robustness experiments are provided, despite the method depending on clustering and iterative optimization. This makes the large reported improvements difficult to assess.

Some claims are overstated. The paper says the method is training-free and prior-free, but it fits GMM parameters, learns adaptive coefficients, uses unlabeled dataset-level inference, and depends on OT marginals. These may still be valid design choices, but the wording overstates what is actually demonstrated.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and useful problem: improving zero-shot classification by combining complementary foundation models rather than adapting a single VLM. The distinction between VLM semantic alignment and VFM visual discriminability is well motivated by the reported clustering and accuracy behavior.

The proposed adaptive OT formulation is simple, training-free in the sense of no gradient fine-tuning, and broadly applicable to black-box or feature-only models. The transductive and inductive variants make the method practically relevant across evaluation settings.

The empirical results are strong and broad: experiments span 11 natural image datasets, 10 remote sensing datasets, and 5 medical pathology datasets. Reported gains are substantial, e.g. on natural transductive classification the best SOTA variant improves the average from 74.5 for GTA-CLIP to 77.8, and on remote sensing and pathology the method improves over strong domain-specific VLM baselines and TransCLIP variants.

The ablations support the central design choices: adding VFM-derived information matters, self-adaptive weighting improves over fixed weighting, and joint optimization improves over disjoint learning. The convergence and efficiency analyses also help establish practicality.
The manuscript is generally clear about the high-level pipeline and includes implementation details such as model choices, preprocessing, entropy parameter, hardware, and complexity.
weaknesses: The main comparisons do not fully isolate the algorithmic contribution from the benefit of adding stronger foundation models. On natural datasets, the CLIP-1+CLIP-2 variant is below the best prior transductive method, while the largest gains come from adding DINOv2/DINOv3. Stronger baselines such as simple averaging/max, calibrated ensembling, GMM-only DINO classifiers, and non-adaptive multi-model OT should be reported consistently in the main tables for the same model sets.

The method is described as prior-free, but the OT problem requires source and target marginals, including a class marginal q. The manuscript does not clearly specify how q is chosen or analyze sensitivity to class imbalance. If q is uniform, the method implicitly assumes balanced classes, which is a meaningful prior and may explain part of the performance on balanced benchmarks.

The optimization and notation have several technical ambiguities. The dimensions of p and q appear swapped between the main text and appendix; the Sinkhorn update and Diag(p) exp(S/epsilon) Diag(q) expression are hard to reconcile with T in R^{N x K}; and the adaptive weight update differs by a factor of 2 between the derivation and algorithm. These may be fixable, but they currently weaken reproducibility and confidence in the derivation.

The VFM GMM component-to-class alignment is underexplained. Since GMM components are permutation-invariant, the paper should clarify how components are initialized and semantically anchored, especially before the coupled updates have reliable assignments. This is central to the claimed ability to use VFMs for zero-shot classification.

The evaluation lacks uncertainty estimates or multiple-run reporting despite using iterative GMM/OT procedures with possible initialization sensitivity. No statistical significance or variance is provided for the reported gains.

Reproducibility is not fully satisfactory: the abstract says the implementation code is available, but the visible manuscript has no actual URL. Dataset templates are deferred to code, and several hyperparameters/initialization choices are insufficiently specified in the paper itself.

Some claims are stronger than the evidence warrants, especially “without hyperparameter adjustment” and broad “prior-free” generalization. The paper would be more convincing with robustness tests for epsilon, class-prior mismatch, number/type of ensemble models, and imbalanced target sets.
